prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, made independently by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider.

statement.case_for: The 2012 observation of the Higgs boson is a clue from nature of the kind I value most: a prediction made in 1964 and woven into the whole Standard Model was tested, and it came out right, in two independent experiments with different detector technologies. The 2013 prize honoured the theory, but a theoretical prize does not close the book on the discovery itself, and the experimental side has now waited fourteen years while Run 2 and Run 3 have measured couplings to third-generation fermions and tightened the picture. Nothing on this shortlist is more securely confirmed or more central to our understanding of why elementary particles have mass. Having looked again at the full set of opening ballots, I still find that few other candidates combine this degree of significance with this degree of maturity. The sharing of credit is a real problem, but the committee has handled collaboration-scale discoveries before by crediting the people who conceived and led the programmes.
statement.case_against: My own preferred prize is also one of the hardest to attribute. Two collaborations of thousands made the discovery, the statutes limit us to three people, and four credited names (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) all have strong claims, so any trio will look arbitrary to part of the community. Opening support is also thin: only three members ranked B046, and Johansson put it seventh. If the committee judges that no individuals can be fairly singled out, the Higgs experiments become the candidate that cannot be awarded rather than the one that should be, and a cleanly attributable prize such as optical lattice clocks would then be the more defensible choice.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the Higgs experiments second, and for the Higgs would name Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra as the founding leaders and the spokesperson at discovery, while conceding that excluding Virdee must be justified.
responses.response: We agree on the two discoveries and mostly on their order, so the difference is mainly about names and about IceCube's maturity. On names, I would keep one leader per experiment plus a second founder, and I think the CMS side carries more weight than your trio gives it. Virdee conceived and led CMS as a project and was its spokesperson through construction, and Della Negra was a co-founder. Taking Gianotti, Della Negra and Virdee gives ATLAS one name and CMS two, and I can defend that. Jenni's founding role in ATLAS is just as strong and I do not think the allocation is settled, so I want the expert reports to decide between the two founders of ATLAS and CMS. On IceCube I accept the diffuse flux as solid, but the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) rest on a few objects at modest significance, and the allocation among Halzen, Spiering and Karle is also open to dispute, since AMANDA and Baikal precursors were credited by others. I keep it as my alternative, not my first choice.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as the clearest precision-atomic case on the list, with a clean Katori and Ye pairing, 1e-18 uncertainties, many independent laboratories and a coming redefinition of the second.
responses.response: The attribution here is better than for any other candidate, and I take that seriously, because B053 is the only top candidate where two names carry the credit with little controversy. My reservation is about discovery content. The 1e-18 level is a magnificent measurement achievement, but I want to know what has been learned about nature. The tests of relativistic redshift over millimetres and searches for drifting constants are so far null results, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. It also comes after the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012) prizes, so the committee should ask whether it is a new step or a late chapter of the same story. I accept that this is not a fatal objection, since a measurement prize can be very fine, and I have therefore listed B053 as an alternative. I would be willing to move toward it if the committee decides the Higgs allocation cannot be settled fairly.

responses.point: Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a surprise from quantum mechanics in a stable 2D material, with a theory-plus-experiment trio (Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero) and many replications.
responses.response: I ranked this fifth, and I still admire it: the continuum model made a precise prediction and the 2018 experiment found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, which is exactly the theory-meets-nature sequence I like. My disagreement with you is on timing. You call the band picture firm and the discovery robust, and I accept that, but the question that makes the superconductivity interesting, namely the pairing mechanism, is still unresolved, and the field is only eight years old. In my experience of how this committee works, prizes for a field still moving this quickly tend to age better if we wait a few more years, because the lasting contribution is not yet clear. I also worry that Cao, Dean and other experimental groups, and earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, make the three-name credit less clean than you suggest. I would not oppose it, but I would not put it ahead of a mature experimental discovery.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, because of its clean general mechanism (the Z2 invariant) and over fifteen years of independent confirmation.
responses.response: I do not dispute the maturity or the importance of the idea, and the Kane and Mele paper is a model of a simple mechanism with wide consequences. My qualification is that I find the attribution harder than you suggest. The decisive HgTe proposal came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not among the credited names, so a prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp rewards a prediction that Molenkamp's experiment actually tested through a different proposal. The 3D strand with Hasan is a separate discovery and the committee would have to decide whether it belongs in the same prize. The 2016 prize for topological phases also makes novelty harder to argue. I think the topological insulator case is strong enough to be a serious contender in a future year, but I am less convinced than you that this configuration of names is the right one.

uncertainties: Which three of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee best represent ATLAS and CMS, and whether the committee considers any individual allocation fair for two collaborations of thousands.
Whether expert reports would show the Higgs experimental credit to be separable enough from the collaborations to withstand criticism.
Whether optical lattice clocks, which most colleagues rank highly, are judged to add a new discovery beyond the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
Whether IceCube source associations are firm enough, and which pioneers of AMANDA and Baikal belong in the credit, if the committee prefers neutrino astronomy.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the Higgs candidates or the other shortlisted names. My Princeton supervisor David Gross and my co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited on any shortlisted ballot, and I have no known institutional tie to ATLAS, CMS or the other candidates beyond general acquaintance within the field.
